sessions.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
script: You're here, and that's already a good step. Maybe your mind is racing right now, running three steps ahead of the day.
For this exercise, keep your eyes open. You can do it sitting or standing, in your kitchen or on a train platform.
Place both feet flat on the floor. Feel the ground holding you, under your heels, under your toes.
Let the air out through your mouth, slowly, as if you were blowing on soup that's too hot.
[pause 3s]
Once more. A long, easy out-breath, without forcing the in-breath at all.
Anxiety likes to live in tomorrow: what might happen, what might go wrong. Your senses only know about now.
So we'll use them like a rope to pull you back here. Five, four, three, two, one. Take your time with each step. There's no rush.
If a thought pulls you toward tomorrow, that's okay. Notice it, and come back to the step you were on.
Start with your eyes. Look for five things you can see.
They don't need to be special. The corner of a table, a power outlet, a mug, the sky through the window.
Rest your gaze on the first one. Look at it as if you had to describe it to someone who has never seen it.
What is its exact color? Not just "white", but off-white, a slightly grey white, a white that shines where the light hits it.
Notice its edges. Are they sharp, rounded, a little worn?
[pause 3s]
Move on to the second thing. Take in its shape, its shadow, the small details you've never noticed. A scratch, a reflection, a speck of dust.
Then the third. And the fourth, maybe a little further away. Let your eyes travel slowly, without hurrying.
And a fifth. If your eyes want to go back to one of them, that's allowed.
[pause 3s]
Now, touch. Find four things you can feel against your skin.
The first may already be there: the weight of your body on the chair, or your feet inside your shoes.
Notice the pressure. Is it stronger on one side than the other? On your heels, or on the balls of your feet?
Second: the fabric of your clothes. On your shoulders, on your thighs. Is it soft, scratchy, snug, light?
For the third, you can place a hand on something. A table, your knee, the armrest. Feel whether it's cool or warm, smooth or rough.
And the fourth, more subtle: the air on your face, on the backs of your hands. Maybe a slight draft, maybe a little warmth.
[pause 3s]
Now, sounds. Listen, and find three of them.
Start with the most obvious one. A car, a voice, the hum of a fridge or a computer.
Then look for a more distant sound, right at the edge of what you can hear. Let your listening widen, as if your ears were opening a little more.
And finally, a sound very close to you. The rustle of your clothes when you move, or the quiet sound of your own breathing.
You don't need to name each sound precisely. Just notice that it's there, then that it changes, or stops.
If a thought slips in among the sounds, let it drift into the background, like a radio playing in the next room.
Now, two smells. This is often the hardest step, so be patient with yourself.
Breathe in gently through your nose, without forcing it. Maybe there's a hint of coffee, laundry soap on your sweater, hand soap on your fingers.
You can bring your wrist or your sleeve up to your nose.

If you can't smell anything in particular, that's completely fine too. Then imagine two smells you love. Warm bread from a bakery in the morning. Freshly cut grass. The peel of an orange you've just opened.
Let the memory of those smells come back, as vividly as you can.
[pause 3s]
And finally, one taste. Notice what's in your mouth right now.
Maybe the trace of your last drink, toothpaste, or just a neutral taste.
Run your tongue over your teeth, along the roof of your mouth. Feel the saliva, the temperature inside your mouth.
If you have a glass of water nearby, you can take a slow sip, and follow its coolness until it fades away.
Each time you explore something with your senses, your attention steps out of the worried story. It's simple, and that's why it helps.
Now come back to your whole body. Your feet on the floor. Your hands resting. Your eyes taking in the room.
Let your out-breath lengthen one more time, easily.
[pause 3s]
Take a moment to notice how you feel, without expecting anything. Maybe your anxiety has dropped a notch, or several. Maybe it's still here, but a little less overwhelming.
If you had to give it a score out of ten right now, what would it be? Simply compare it with earlier, without judging the number.
If nothing has changed, that isn't a failure. You spent a few minutes here, instead of in tomorrow. That's exactly what the practice is.
Keep this method in your pocket. In a waiting room, before a phone call, in the middle of a restless night, it's always available. It asks for nothing more than what's already around you.
Five things seen, four touched, three heard, two smelled, one tasted.
Before you go back to your day, choose one of the things you saw earlier, and look at it one last time. Let it be your little reminder: here and now is where you actually live.

sessions.title: Before a party or a date
script: In a few hours, or maybe a few minutes, you'll be meeting people. A party, a dinner, a first date. And something inside you is tightening.
Maybe your throat, your stomach, slightly clammy hands. Maybe that little voice suggesting you cancel.
All of this is deeply human. Feeling nervous before seeing people doesn't mean you're strange, or that the evening will go badly. It just means it matters to you.
So, to begin, there's nothing to fix. Just a little room for what you're feeling.
Settle in wherever you are, sitting or standing. You can keep your eyes open, or let them half close.
If your heart is beating fast, let it beat. That's your body getting ready, like before a game or an exam. There's nothing dangerous about it.
First, we'll talk to the body, because the body is what sounded the alarm.
Breathe in calmly through your nose, no bigger than usual.
Then breathe out through your mouth, slowly, as if you were fogging up a window. Let the out-breath last longer than the in-breath.
[pause 3s]
Once more. Breathe in, normally. And breathe out, long and soft, all the way to the end.
[pause 3s]
Now look at your hands. If they're clenched, open them. Gently spread your fingers, then let them fall back, loose, onto your thighs.
Notice the warmth coming back into your palms. Let your shoulders drop half an inch. Unclench your jaw, let your tongue rest.
One last long out-breath, and let your body sink a little into the seat.
Breathing out slowly is a simple way of telling your nervous system it can slow down. You don't have to believe it. You just have to do it.
[pause 3s]
Now let's see what your mind is doing. There's a good chance it's already playing a little movie.
The moment you walk in and nobody talks to you. The awkward silence. The joke that falls flat. The other person's bored expression.
These images feel real, and the body reacts to them as if they were.
Yet they all have one thing in common: none of them has happened yet. They're predictions.
So try something. Each time one of these scenarios plays, simply say to yourself, silently: "prediction".
"They'll think I'm boring." Prediction. "I'm going to blush." Prediction. "I won't know what to say." Prediction.
You're not trying to prove it's false. You're just noticing that it's a guess your brain is making, not a fact.
[pause 3s]
And remember the times you dreaded an evening, and it actually went well, or at least better than you expected. Your brain tends to forget those.
Tonight, too, there's a good chance reality will be simpler than the movie.
Here's something many people find reassuring. Tonight, most of the people you meet will mostly be thinking about… themselves.
About their outfit, about what they're going to say, about that person they don't know. Some of them will have the same knot in their stomach that you do.
Psychologists even have a name for it: the spotlight effect. We feel like we're under the stage lights, when in fact other people notice us far less than we think.
You're not on stage. You're one person among other people, all of whom would like to have a nice time.
And if you blush, or search for your words, most people won't even notice. The ones who do often find it rather endearing.
So let's change the goal. Instead of trying to come across well, to be funny, interesting, perfect, try a lighter intention: curiosity.
Being curious about at least one person. Who they are, what lights them up, how they see things.
When your attention goes out toward someone else, it steps away from that spotlight pointed at you. And awkwardness often loosens its grip.
Put this intention into your own words. For example: "Tonight, I want to get to know someone." Or: "Tonight, I'm listening."
[pause 3s]
To make it easier, prepare one simple question you can pull out of your pocket if a silence settles in.
An open question, one that invites a story. "What's been keeping you busy lately?" "How do you know everyone here?" "What's the best thing you did this summer?"
Pick one. Say it once in your head, in your own voice, calmly.
Now picture the person answering, and you listening, really listening, nodding along. Nothing else to get right.
[pause 3s]
One small gesture for the moment you arrive. Just before you ring the bell or push the door open, pause for two seconds. Feel your feet in your shoes, open your hands, and let out a long breath.
Then walk in and look for a first face to smile at. You don't need to shine. A hello, a name, your question, and you're on your way.
And if a silence happens anyway, it's not a disaster. You can take a sip, smile, or ask your question. Silences are part of every conversation.
Come back to your breath. A long out-breath. Hands open. Feet grounded.

And keep one last thing in mind: you're allowed to leave whenever you want. If after an hour you've had enough, you can say goodbye and go home. That's allowed, and it doesn't make you any less likeable.
Knowing the door is open often makes it easier to walk through it.
You're going with your nerves, your question, and your curiosity. That's more than enough.

sessions.title: Meet your emotion
script: Welcome to this moment for yourself. There may be an emotion keeping you company today, and you've chosen to stop and look at it, rather than run from it. That takes courage.
Get comfortable, with your back supported and your feet on the floor. You can close your eyes, or rest your gaze on a spot on the floor.
Take two or three breaths that are a little fuller than usual, and let each out-breath set you down a little more into your seat.
[pause 3s]
Now feel your body breathing on its own. Your belly rising slightly, the air a little cooler as it enters your nose. Stay here for a few moments, just with this movement.
If your mind is already wandering, that's normal. Just bring it back to the feeling of air moving in and out.
We're going to practice RAIN, a four-step way of moving through a hard emotion without drowning in it. R for recognize. A for allow. I for investigate. N for nurture.

This approach was popularized by the American psychologist Tara Brach. The idea is simple: instead of pushing away what you feel, you make room for it, one step at a time. And often, it becomes easier to bear.

To practice, choose a situation that stirs you up a little, but not the heaviest thing in your life. Tension with a coworker, a message that went unanswered, a worry about someone. Something in the middle, a five out of ten.
Let the scene come to you. Where were you, who was there, what was said? Just enough for the feeling to wake up.
[pause 3s]
First step: recognize. Simply ask yourself: what's happening inside me, right now?
Let a word come. Worry. Disappointment. Anger. Shame. Sadness. There may be several, tangled together like threads.
You can say it silently, in a calm voice, like a friend noticing: "ah, there's anger here", or "oh, that's fear".
If no word comes, just describe what you notice: "something tight", "restlessness", "a heaviness". That's just as accurate.
Naming isn't solving yet. It's simply turning on the light in the room.
[pause 3s]
Second step: allow. This doesn't mean you approve of the situation, or that you like what you're feeling.
It means stopping, just for a moment, the fight against the fact that it's here. Like when it rains: you don't have to love the rain, but there's no point shouting at the sky.
You can whisper inside: "yes, this is here". Or "okay, I see you".
Notice if there's resistance, an urge to think about something else, to justify yourself, to blame yourself for feeling this way. You can let that be, too. Yes, that too.
Often, it's the fight against an emotion that wears us out the most. When we stop pushing against the door, it sometimes weighs a little less.
[pause 3s]
Third step: investigate, with kindness. Now we leave the story behind and move toward the body.
Where does this emotion live? Take a little tour. Your throat, maybe tight. Your chest, heavy or pressed. Your stomach, knotted. Your shoulders, your jaw, your hands.
Choose the place where it's clearest, and rest your attention there, gently, the way you'd rest a hand on someone's shoulder.
Explore it with curiosity. Is it warm or cool? Hard like a stone, or shifting? Does it have a size, a shape, edges?
Notice, too, what the emotion is pushing you to do. Withdraw? Snap at someone? Grab your phone so you don't have to think about it? You don't have to follow that push. Just see it.
If it gets too intense, you can come back to your breath or your feet on the floor at any moment. You're the one in charge.
[pause 3s]
Then ask this part of you, kindly: "what are you afraid of?" Or: "what do you need me to understand?"
Don't look for the right answer. Listen to whatever comes, a sentence, an image, or nothing at all. Simply asking is already a form of care.
Sometimes the answer turns up later, during the day or on a walk. You've already done your part by asking.
Fourth step: nurture. Now ask yourself: what do I need, right here, right now? To be reassured? To be understood? To know it's not my fault? A bit of rest?
When you have an idea, even a vague one, try to offer it to yourself.
You can place a hand on your heart, or on the spot where the emotion is. Feel the warmth of your palm, the light pressure.
And offer yourself a few words, the ones you'd say to a friend going through the same thing. "Of course this is hard." "I'm here." "You're doing your best."
If the words ring false, imagine instead someone who loves you, or once did, saying them to you, in their own voice.
And if what you need is more practical, a break, a phone call, a glass of water, a boundary to set, make a note of it somewhere inside. You can give it to yourself later.
[pause 3s]
Let these words, or this gesture, do their quiet work. There's nothing to force.
Notice even the smallest change: a shoulder softening, a slightly longer breath, warmth under your hand.
Now let go of all the steps. Nothing left to do, nothing left to explore.
Simply rest in being aware. There's the emotion, maybe softer, maybe the same. There are the sounds, the breath, the feeling of the seat beneath you.
And there's you, noticing all of it. A bit like the sky, which holds the clouds without becoming the clouds.
You are not your anger, or your fear. You're the space they move through.
This emotion is a visitor. It arrived, it's shifting, and sooner or later it will leave, like every one that came before it.
[pause 3s]
Notice how you feel now, without looking for a result. Sometimes RAIN brings real relief. Sometimes, just a little more gentleness. Both count.
Gently, come back to the room. Move your fingers, your shoulders. Let the sounds around you come in.
Open your eyes when the moment feels right for you.
The next time an emotion floods you during the day, you don't need all the steps. Sometimes, pausing and saying "yes, this is here" is enough to shift something.

sessions.title: Urge surfing
script: If you're starting this session, maybe an urge is here, right now. The urge to pick up your phone, open the cupboard, light a cigarette, check your messages one more time.
That makes this the perfect moment. You don't need to wait until you're calm: we practice precisely while the urge is here.
And if there's no urge at the moment, remember the last time it was strong, and let the memory of it come back a little.
Sit down with your feet flat on the floor. If the object of your urge is within reach, move it a little further away, or turn it face down, just for the length of this session.
You haven't promised anything. You're not giving anything up forever. You're observing for a few minutes, that's all.
If part of you feels it's hopeless, that you'll give in anyway, that's okay. You can do this exercise with that doubt along for the ride.
Take a slow breath in, and let the air flow out easily.
[pause 3s]
Start by giving this urge a name. Simply: "urge to scroll". "Urge for something sweet". "Urge to smoke". "Urge to check".
Then ask yourself: what is it promising me? Often, it's not the thing itself. It's a break. A reward. A little forgetting. The end of some discomfort.
"Follow me, and you'll feel better." Listen to that promise, without believing it, without arguing. Just hear it.
And maybe notice what set it off: tiredness, boredom, tension, an unpleasant email. Urges rarely come out of nowhere.
Spotting the trigger is already useful. Next time, you might answer the real need instead: rest, move, take a breather.
[pause 3s]
Now look for where the urge lives in your body. Because an urge isn't just an idea. It's also a collection of sensations.
Maybe restlessness in your hands, fingers that want to move. Tension in your jaw. A hollow feeling in your stomach. Warmth in your chest, your mouth watering, impatience in your legs.
Take time to do the full tour. Where is it strongest?
And give its intensity a score from one to ten. One is barely there. Ten is almost irresistible. Remember that number.
[pause 3s]
Here's the image we'll use. Imagine your urge is a wave, out at sea.
Every wave has the same life. It forms, it swells, it reaches a peak, then it breaks and dissolves onto the sand. No wave rises forever.
Urges often work the same way. Many people notice that they peak and then fade within a few minutes, if they aren't fed.
When we give in right away, we never get to see the wave go down on its own. So the brain comes to believe the urge is an order. Today, you're showing it something different.
Your breath is your surfboard. You don't need to stop the wave, or throw yourself into it. Just stay standing on the board, and let it carry you.
[pause 3s]
Bring your attention to your breathing. Air coming in, air going out. Let the out-breath be a little longer, like your balance settling.
And at the same time, keep an eye on the place in your body where the urge is showing up.
Maybe it's rising right now. The sensations grow stronger, the thoughts speed up: "just this once", "it doesn't count", "come on, quickly".
Those thoughts are part of the wave. You can hear them, like the sound of the water, without answering them.
Stay on your board. Breathe in. Breathe out. You have nothing else to do.
If you catch yourself bargaining, telling yourself "fine, right after the session", notice it with a little smile. That's the wave talking too.
[pause 3s]
Observe closely. Does the sensation pulse, or is it steady? Does it move around? Does it have a shape, a temperature?
The closer you look, the more the urge becomes a set of small, shifting sensations, rather than a command you can't refuse.
If the urge is very strong, remember: it's uncomfortable, but it isn't dangerous. You can ride it out.
Your body knows how to do this. A sensation, even a strong one, rarely stays at its peak for very long. Sooner or later, it moves, it changes.
At some point, the wave reaches its peak. You might feel it: a moment where it's at its most intense, and then a slight shift.
If you're there now, this is the time to be especially gentle with yourself. Feet on the floor, long out-breath. You're still standing.
You can count your out-breaths, one, two, three, up to five, and then start again. Each out-breath is a small paddle stroke that keeps you balanced on the crest.
If your hands are fidgeting, lay them flat on your thighs and feel their warmth. Give your body something simple to do while the wave rolls beneath you.
[pause 3s]
And then, almost without warning, the wave starts to go down. The tension eases a little. The thoughts slow down. The urgency loses its voice.
Follow this ebb with the same curiosity you gave the rise. Where does your body relax first? Your hands? Your jaw? Your stomach?
If the urge rises again, that's normal, the sea has more than one wave. You simply climb back on your board and start surfing again.
With practice, many people find the waves get a little lower, or come a little less often. But today, it's just about this one.
Now rate the intensity again, from one to ten. Compare it with your number from the beginning.
Maybe it's dropped a lot, maybe just one point. Maybe it has changed shape. All of this is valuable information: your urge isn't a straight line, it's a movement.
[pause 3s]
And here's the heart of it. You didn't have to fight, or obey. You watched.
Now you can choose freely. Maybe you'll set the urge aside. Maybe you'll still have that square of chocolate, but you'll really savor it, by choice rather than on autopilot.
Both options belong to you. The goal isn't perfection. The goal is to put some space back between the urge and the action. And you've just created that space.
Every wave you surf makes the next one a little more familiar.
Take one last breath, feel your feet, look around you, and pick up the thread of your day.

sessions.title: Leaves on a stream
script: Welcome. Take a moment to really arrive, right where you are.
Settle into a position where your body can stay still for a few minutes. Sitting, with your back upright but not stiff, or lying down if you prefer.
Let your eyes close, or lower your gaze toward the floor, slightly unfocused.
There's nothing to get right in these few minutes. Just be here, sitting, and watching.
Breathe normally. Simply notice the air coming in, and the air going out.
Maybe your breathing is fast, maybe slow. There's nothing to correct. Let it do whatever it wants.
Feel the places where your body is supported: the backs of your thighs, your back against the chair, your hands resting. Each out-breath settles you in a little more.
[pause 3s]
Today, we're going to practice something simple and yet precious: looking at your thoughts, instead of looking through them.
Usually, when a thought like "I'm going to mess this up" shows up, we take it as reality. We're inside it, like wearing glasses we've forgotten we have on.
This exercise comes from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. It invites you to take those glasses off and set them on the table for a few moments, so you can look at them.
The goal isn't to chase thoughts away, or to make them more pleasant. It's to change your relationship with them: watching them pass, instead of being swept along.
Imagine you're sitting beside a small stream. Choose whatever place comes to you: a country brook, a mountain river, the edge of a canal in the city.
Notice what's beneath you. Grass, a flat stone, a wooden bench. Feel the temperature of the air on your skin. Maybe a little sunshine, maybe cool shade.
Listen to the water. It flows at its own pace, not too fast, not too slow. It makes a small, steady sound against the pebbles.
[pause 3s]
And on this water, leaves are floating by. Every so often, a leaf drifts in from the left, glides past you, and moves off to the right, until it disappears around a bend in the stream.
All kinds of leaves. Green, yellow, russet, large or tiny. Watch one or two float past, without doing anything.
[pause 3s]
Now gently turn your attention to what's happening in your mind.
Each time a thought appears, take it and place it on a leaf. Then let the leaf carry it away.

If the thought is made of words, you can imagine those words written on the leaf. "I need to call the mechanic back." Onto a leaf. If it's an image, place the image on the leaf, like a small photograph.
Every thought gets its own leaf. Worries, shopping lists, memories, brilliant ideas, judgments, questions.
You don't sort them. You don't keep the good ones or chase away the bad ones. Everything goes onto the water, in the same way.
[pause 3s]
Let each leaf go at its own pace. You don't need to push the current to make it go faster. And you don't need to hold it back to look at it longer.
Some thoughts will come back. The same worry, five leaves later. That's perfectly fine. Place it down again, without irritation. The stream never gets tired.
If several thoughts arrive at once, put them all on one big leaf, or on several small ones. It's up to you.
And if there are no thoughts for a while, simply watch the water flow. The quiet stretches are part of the stream too.
At some point, and it's almost certain, you'll realize you're no longer by the stream. A thought hooked you, you followed it, and now you're preparing tomorrow's meeting or replaying a conversation.
This is exactly the heart of the exercise. The moment you notice is a small moment of waking up.
Without scolding yourself, come back to the water's edge. Take the thought that pulled you away, and place it, too, on a leaf.
[pause 3s]
There are also quiet thoughts, ones we don't even recognize as thoughts. "I can't do this." "This doesn't work for me." "This is a bit silly."
They're thoughts like any others. They deserve their leaf. Watch them float away.

Sometimes a thought comes back with real force, sticky, insistent. "What if I can't pay the bills this month?" Notice how it tugs at you. You can even give it a bigger, heavier leaf. It still floats. It just takes a little longer to drift away.
Notice, too, the thoughts that comment on the exercise: "Am I doing this right?" "My stream isn't realistic enough." One leaf for each.
And if an emotion shows up, impatience, boredom, a touch of sadness, you can name it, and place it on the water too.
The more you practice this, the more natural it becomes to tell yourself: oh, that's a thought. Not a truth, not an order. Just a thought.
Now carry on at your own pace, with shorter guidance from me. One thought, one leaf. The water flowing.
A thought arrives. You notice it. You place it on a leaf. And you watch it drift away, at the pace of the water.
[pause 5s]
If you've wandered off, no problem at all. Come back to the bank, one leaf, and the current.

If you're having trouble seeing the leaves, that's fine. Some people imagine bubbles rising instead, or clouds crossing the sky. The image doesn't matter much. What matters is the gesture: notice, place, let go.
Notice that while the leaves pass, you stay on the bank. You're the one watching, not the leaf.
Thoughts come and go. You're here before, during, and after each one of them.
The bank doesn't leave with the current. It stays right where it is, steady, while the water flows by.
Maybe the stream is very crowded right now, with leaves everywhere. Or maybe there are long stretches with nothing at all. Either way, just watch the water.
If the current seems to stop, or a leaf gets stuck, notice that. It's often a sign that a small thought is here: "the leaf isn't moving". Place that thought, too, on another leaf.
[pause 4s]
Gently, let the image of the stream fade. The leaves carry on their journey without you, and that's just fine.
Come back to your breath. To the points where you're supported. To the weight of your hands.
Become aware of the room around you, and the sounds that are here.
Feel the air coming in through your nose, a little cooler, and flowing back out a little warmer.
Take a moment to notice what has changed, if anything. Maybe a little more space between you and whatever passes through you. As if your thoughts were stuck a little less tightly to you.
You may have had lots of thoughts, and been carried off often. That doesn't mean you failed. Every return to the bank was the exercise.
Gently move your fingers, your feet. Stretch if your body feels like it. And open your eyes, in your own time.
Today, when a thought gets loud, remember this little phrase: "I notice I'm having the thought that…". It's a leaf. You can let it drift.

sessions.title: Name it to tame it
script: Welcome. This session will teach you a very simple tool you can take anywhere: putting a word on what's happening.
Sit with your back upright but not rigid, your hands resting on your thighs or one in the other.
Close your eyes if that feels okay, or lower your gaze toward the floor.
Let your body take its place. Shoulders dropping, face softening, belly letting go.
Let go of the idea of doing it well, too. There's nothing to achieve here, only things to notice.
To begin, rest your attention on your breath, wherever you feel it most clearly. Maybe at the tip of your nose, maybe in your chest, maybe in your belly rising and falling.
Follow one in-breath from beginning to end. Then one out-breath, all the way to the little resting moment that follows it.
You can already try, very gently, noting the breath itself. "Rising" on the in-breath. "Falling" on the out-breath. Just to get a feel for the idea.
[pause 3s]
Your breath will be your point of return, your home base. Every time you drift away from it, you can come back.
Here's how mental noting works. When something pulls your attention away from the breath, you notice it, and you give it a word. Just one. Simple and soft.
For example, a door closing: "hearing". An itch: "sensation". A thought about your to-do list: "planning".
Then, without lingering, you come back to the breath.
Think of it like a light tap on the shoulder: you notice, you name, and you let go.
One word every few seconds is plenty. This isn't a labeling race. Between two notes, there's the breath, calm, carrying on.
The word doesn't need to be perfect. It's just a way of acknowledging: "ah, this is what's happening". Say it silently, in a calm, almost tender tone, the way you'd greet a neighbor on the stairs.
Many people find that naming what they're experiencing helps them step back a little. You're no longer inside the thought; you're watching it pass.
Researchers have observed that putting feelings into words can soften their intensity a little. That's what we'll explore today, lightly.
[pause 3s]
Let's start with the body. Stay with the breath, and let sensations show up.
Maybe the contact of your hands on your thighs. You can note: "touch".
Maybe warmth in your palms or at the back of your neck: "warmth". A little coolness on your face: "cool".
A tingling in your foot: "tingling". Tension in your back: "tension".
Each time, one word, and back to the breath. No need to analyze it, or change the sensation.

If a sensation is unpleasant, discomfort in your knee, stiffness in your neck, you can note that too: "discomfort", "stiffness". Then see whether it changes by itself. Often it pulses, shifts, eases a little.
[pause 3s]
Now open your listening to sounds. When a sound reaches you, simply note: "hearing".
You don't need to say "car", "bird", or "neighbor". Just "hearing". The sound arrives, you note it, it leaves.
Notice how sounds appear and disappear without any help from you. Hearing. Back to the breath. Hearing. Back.
Notice, too, the silence between two sounds. If it comes naturally, you can note it: "silence".
If you find yourself waiting for the next sound, listening out for it, you can note: "waiting". Then come back to the breath.
[pause 3s]
Now, thoughts. This is often where anxiety hides, so it's an important step.
When a thought carries you off, try to see what kind it is. If you're preparing something, organizing your week, making a list: "planning".
If you're picturing what could go wrong: "worrying". If you're telling yourself you're doing this wrong, or that someone else was wrong: "judging".
If you're replaying a memory: "remembering". If you're making up a scene: "imagining".
The word creates a little distance. "Worrying" is no longer "something terrible is going to happen". It's just your mind doing what minds do.
And when you don't know what to call it, "thinking" is more than enough.
Sometimes you only notice the thought after a minute, after a whole journey. That doesn't matter at all. Note it wherever you find it, and come back.
And notice the effect of the word. Does the thought keep the same strength once it's been named, or does it deflate a little?
[pause 3s]
Now, emotions. They often blend with thoughts and sensations. When you notice one, give it its name.
A clenching that feels like fear: "fear". Impatience, irritation: "irritation". A light heaviness: "sadness". A gentle moment: "calm", or "joy".
You can feel them in the body, too. Fear in the stomach, irritation in the shoulders. Note the emotion, then come back to the breath.
There's no wrong emotion to note. They all have the right to be here, for as long as they last.
If an emotion is strong, you can note it several times, slowly, in rhythm with the breath. "Fear… fear…" Like a hand resting on the shoulder of someone who's trembling.
[pause 3s]
Now we bring it all together. The breath is still your home base. And anything that pulls you away from it, sensation, sound, thought or emotion, gets its little word.
I'll speak less now. If you get lost for a long time, that's fine. The moment you notice, you can even note "lost", or "returning". And you return.
[pause 3s]
Touch. Hearing. Planning. Breathing.
If you're noting too quickly, slow down. Let the breath make at least one full round between two words.
Keep your words light. If you catch yourself searching for the exact word for ten seconds, just note "searching", and smile.
Sometimes nothing shows up. The breath is simply here. You can note "breathing", or note nothing at all.
Breathing. Hearing. Thinking. Returning.
[pause 3s]
If the same thought keeps coming back, you can note it each time, with the same gentleness. "Worrying." "Worrying." It often ends up losing its momentum.
And if you realize you're noting in a harsh, impatient voice, soften your tone. The word matters less than the kindness you place it with.
Maybe notice the pleasant moments too. A softening in your shoulders, a moment of calm. They deserve their word as well: "ease", "calm".
Now let go of the technique. No more noting. Simply let things appear and disappear, without naming them.
Maybe notice how everything moves. Sensations, sounds, thoughts: nothing stays in place for very long.
You simply stay here, in the middle of whatever passes through. No need to grab hold of anything.
Take a moment to feel how you are now. Maybe a little more space. Maybe not. That's okay.
Gently come back to the room. Feel your feet, your hands, your back. Take a slightly deeper breath, and stretch if you feel like it.
Open your eyes when the moment feels right for you.
You can practice this anywhere: on the train, in a queue, while walking. A few words, a few breaths, and you get a little perspective back.
During your day, when anxiety rises, you can take back just one word. "Fear." "Worrying." Simply saying it inside can remind you that you can watch the storm, without being the storm.

sessions.title: Living with uncertainty
script: Waiting is one of the hardest things there is. Waiting for test results, for an answer after a job interview, for news about someone you love, for a decision that isn't up to you.
Time seems to stretch. Your phone becomes a magnet. And your mind just won't stop searching.

If you're going through one of these times, know this first: what you're feeling is normal. The human brain doesn't like uncertainty; it often experiences it as a threat. This isn't a flaw in you. It's part of being human.
This session won't give you the answer. But it can help you inhabit the waiting a little differently.
It can help you stay with "I don't know", without rushing to fill it with stories you make up.
[pause 3s]
Get comfortable. Sitting or lying down, whatever feels right. If you can, put your phone away for these few minutes, or turn it face down on the table.
Close your eyes if you like, or keep a soft gaze resting in front of you.
And let your shoulders drop a little. They may have been carrying this waiting all day.
Start by noticing your breathing, just as it is. Maybe it's short, high up in your chest. That often happens when we're waiting.
Without forcing anything, let the out-breath lengthen a little. Like a slow sigh, gently emptying your lungs.
[pause 3s]
Once more. The in-breath comes on its own. The out-breath takes its time.
[pause 3s]
Now place a hand on your belly, if that's comfortable. Feel it rise under your palm, then fall again.
This movement doesn't depend on any answer. It's here, now, faithful. You can lean on it.
If at any point focusing on your breath feels uncomfortable, just let it go back to normal, and bring your attention to your feet instead.
Lengthening your out-breath is a concrete way of signaling to your body that it can ease off its vigilance a little. Nothing to achieve, just let it happen.
Now observe what your mind is doing with this waiting. Let it talk for a bit, without following it.
Maybe it's producing scenarios. The worst ones first: "what if it's serious", "what if they never call back", "what if everything falls apart".
Maybe perfect scenarios too, ones you don't dare believe in. Or endless calculations: "if they didn't call yesterday, that must mean…". "If she said that, it means…".
Maybe you're replaying conversations, hunting for clues, checking again and again.

Notice what these thoughts do in your body, too. A knot in your stomach, raised shoulders, a need to move, to refresh your inbox, to call someone and talk it through one more time. That's the waiting making itself felt. Nothing abnormal.
Just notice that they're here. The way you'd watch cars go by from a window.
[pause 3s]
All these scenarios have something in common. They're your mind's attempts to get back in control.
When we don't know, it feels as if imagining every possibility will make us ready. As if it will hurt less if the worst happens. As if thinking hard enough is already a kind of doing.
It's a touching intention, really. Your mind is trying to protect you.
But you may have noticed that these scenarios don't bring the answer any closer. They make you live through things ten times over that may never happen at all.
You can thank your mind for its efforts. "Thank you, I can see you're trying to help." And gently tell it that, for now, it can rest a little.
Another approach: each time a scenario arrives, call it by name. "Ah, the disaster movie." "Ah, the clue hunt." Recognizing it means you're already not quite inside it.
[pause 3s]
Here's a sentence I'd like you to try. Repeat it silently, slowly, in rhythm with your breath.
"I don't know yet."
[pause 3s]
"And I can stay with that."
[pause 3s]
Notice what these words do in your body. Maybe a slight resistance, as if part of you were protesting: "no, I need to know". That's normal. You can welcome that protest too.
Maybe also a small loosening. As if, for the first time in days, you didn't have to find the answer right away.
Say it again, in your own words if you prefer. "I don't know, it's uncomfortable, and I'm still here."
"I don't know" isn't an empty space you have to fill. It's a space you can breathe in, while you wait.
You can feel this "I don't know" like an open hand. You're not squeezing the future to force it to answer. You're letting it come, whenever it comes.
If your mind comes back with a new "what if", that's normal. You don't have to win against it. Just return to the sentence, at your own pace.
[pause 3s]
Now let's turn toward what is certain. Not what will happen tomorrow, but what is here, right now.
What's certain is that you're breathing. Feel the air come in, and go out.
What's certain is that your body is supported. The chair, the bed, the floor. Feel the weight you're trusting them with.
What's certain are the sounds around you. The hum of an appliance, a car, distant voices. Listen to them for a few moments.
What's certain is the temperature of the air on your hands, the texture of your clothes, the light behind your eyelids.
What's certain is this exact moment. This one. It doesn't hold the answer yet, and yet it's livable. You're living it right now.
[pause 3s]
And there are other certainties, deeper ones. The people who matter to you. The hard times you've already been through, even when you didn't know how they would end.
Remember a period of waiting, in the past, that came to an end. One way or another, you faced it. You found resources.
Whatever answer arrives, you'll still have those resources to meet it. And you don't need to prepare for it completely today.
Take a moment to feel that steadiness. Maybe in your back, in your feet, in the way you're sitting. You've held on before, and you're holding on now.
Finally, let's think about the waiting itself. It may last a few more hours, or a few more days. And that time belongs to you too.
Ask yourself: what could I do today that would be useful or enjoyable, even a little?
A walk around the neighborhood. Calling someone who makes you laugh. Clearing out a drawer. Cooking something simple. Moving forward on a small project. Watching a movie you know by heart.
Choose one thing, just one. Picture yourself doing it. The place, the movements, how it feels.
This isn't running away. It's a way of living during the waiting, instead of putting your life on hold.

And if the urge to check is strong, you can set specific times to look at your messages, say at noon and at six. In between, your phone can stay in another room. It's a way of giving the waiting some structure.
You can also write your worries down on a piece of paper once a day, then fold it away. They don't disappear, but they have a place, somewhere other than your head.
Come back to your breath, and to your hand on your belly if it's still there.
Be gentle with yourself during this time. If you're sleeping less well, if you have less patience, that's understandable. You're carrying something heavy, even if no one can see it.
And if the waiting becomes too heavy to carry alone, you're allowed to talk about it. A friend, someone close, or a professional can help you through it.
Notice how you feel, without demanding anything. The uncertainty may still be here, but you've spent a few minutes breathing with it, instead of fighting it.
Gently, move your fingers and toes. Open your eyes when the moment feels right for you.
And each time your mind slips back into its scenarios today, you can return to these two sentences. I don't know yet. And I can stay with that.

sessions.title: Set your worries down
script: Some days, your head feels like an overstuffed bag. You've crammed in worries about work, money, health, family, and you carry it everywhere, even to bed.
This moment is here to open that bag, look at what's inside, and sort through it. Keep what you can act on. Set the rest down, at least for a while.
Get comfortable, sitting or lying down. Let your hands rest wherever they feel good.
You can close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on the floor.
If you're rushed or restless, that's completely fine. You don't need to be calm to start sorting.
Breathe in through your nose, calmly.
And let the air flow out through your mouth, a little longer, like an end-of-the-day sigh.
[pause 3s]
Once more. Breathe in. And breathe out, feeling your shoulders drop with the air.
[pause 3s]
Now let your breath find its own rhythm. Feel the weight of your body, the contact with the seat or the mattress. For the next few minutes, you have nothing else to do but sort, calmly.

This sorting draws on a very old idea, found in the Stoic philosophers as well as in today's therapies: telling apart what depends on us from what doesn't. It sounds simple, and yet it can lighten the load a lot.
Let your current worries come up. Not to solve them right now. Just to take them out of the bag and set them in front of you.
A first one may show up straight away. Give it a short name. "The overdue report." "The doctor's appointment." "My daughter's grades."
Once it's here, notice where it shows up in your body. A weight on your chest, a clenched jaw, a knotted stomach. Each worry often has its own little corner.
[pause 3s]
Then a second. And maybe a third. Big or small, it doesn't matter. A bill, an argument, a loved one's health, the state of the world.
Three or four is enough for today. You don't need to empty the whole bag.
[pause 3s]
Now imagine two circles drawn on the ground in front of you, as if in chalk.
A small circle in the middle: this is what depends on you. Your actions, your words, your choices, the way you take care of yourself.
And around it, a large circle: what doesn't depend on you. Other people's decisions, the past, the distant future, the weather, the economy, what people think.
That large circle is often the one that fills our nights. And it's exactly the one we have the least control over.
Take a moment to see these two circles clearly. Their color, their size, the surface they're drawn on.
You can even step into the center of the small circle. Feel your feet inside it. This is your ground, the place where your hands can actually do something.
[pause 3s]
Pick up your first worry. Hold it in your hands, like an object. And ask yourself one simple question: is there something I can concretely do about this?
If yes, place it in the small circle. If not, place it in the large one.
Often, a worry has a bit of both. The doctor's appointment, for example: the result doesn't depend on you, but booking the appointment and preparing your questions does.
In that case, split it in two, and place each piece in its own circle.

A difficult bill, for example: the amount is fixed, but calling to ask for a payment plan is up to you. A loved one's health: you can't control it, but you can call them tonight and tell them you're thinking of them.
[pause 3s]
Do the same with the second worry. Then the third. Take your time. There are no wrong answers, only your honesty with yourself.

Notice what happens when you place a worry in the large circle. Sometimes a small relief, as if you were finally admitting it was never your job. Sometimes resistance: "if I stop thinking about it, something bad will happen". And yet, thinking about something is not the same as controlling it.
If you're unsure about a worry, set it on the line between the two circles, and come back to it later. The sorting doesn't need to be perfect.
Now look at the small circle. This is where your strength lies.
Choose just one worry in this circle. And ask yourself: what would the next small action be? Not the whole problem. Just the first step.
Sending that email. Jotting down three ideas on a piece of paper. Calling a friend for advice. Booking a time slot. Sometimes the most useful action is simply going to bed at a reasonable hour.
Once you've found it, picture yourself doing it. When, where, how. Feel what it's like to go from "I'm worried" to "I'm handling it".
If you can, pick a specific moment. Tomorrow at ten, before you open your inbox. The more concrete the step, the more easily your mind can let go of it at night.
[pause 3s]
Now turn toward the large circle. Everything in it, you may have been carrying for days, even weeks. And yet carrying it hasn't changed it.
We're going to set it down. Imagine a place for that: a big wooden box by a fireplace, a rowboat tied up at the edge of a lake, a trunk in an attic. Choose whatever speaks to you.
Take the first worry from the large circle. Feel its weight in your hands. Then gently place it there.
You're not throwing it away. You're not pretending it doesn't exist. You're simply recognizing that it isn't yours to hold, right now.
If you chose the box, hear the soft knock of wood as the worry touches the bottom. If it's the rowboat, watch it drift out a little on the still water, held by its rope.
[pause 3s]
And the next one. Set it down. Maybe notice a slight easing in your arms, your shoulders, your chest.
If a worry resists, if your hands don't want to let go, that's okay. Set it halfway down. Or tell it: "I'll pick you up later, if I need to."
And if it comes knocking again tomorrow, that will be normal. You can set it down again, as many times as it takes.
Once everything is set down, gently close the lid. Or let the rowboat rock at the end of its rope. Your worries are there, sheltered. They don't need you in order to exist.
Take a moment to feel your empty hands. Open them, if you like, palms facing up. They can rest now too.
Now come back to your breath. Notice the space around you, now that your hands are lighter.
Breathe in, and feel your chest open a little. Breathe out, and let your body settle.
Breathe into this freed-up space. There's nothing to fill it with. It's just a little room for you.
Breathe in for a count of four, calmly. And breathe out for a count of six, without forcing. If counting bothers you, drop the numbers and simply keep the out-breath a little longer.
Once more. Four to breathe in. Six to breathe out. And let your shoulders drop a little further each time.
If you feel dizzy or uncomfortable, go straight back to your natural breathing.
[pause 3s]
Notice how you feel now. Maybe a little lighter. Maybe just clearer about what's ahead. The worries haven't disappeared, but they've been put away.
Gently, start to come back. Move your hands, your feet. Stretch if you feel like it.
Remember your small action, the one from the small circle. It's waiting for you, within reach.
You can write it down on paper or in your phone as soon as you open your eyes, so your mind doesn't have to hold on to it.
And for everything else, remember that box by the fire. It's always there, ready to hold what you don't have to carry.
You can do this sorting again whenever the bag fills up. A few minutes is often enough to see more clearly.
Open your eyes when the moment feels right for you.

sessions.title: When sadness visits
script: Maybe sadness is here today. A tiredness of the heart, a heaviness that won't lift, the loss of something or someone, or just a grey day without any clear reason.
First of all, you don't need to feel better right away. This session isn't here to cheer you up at all costs. It's here to keep you company.
You're allowed to be sad. You're allowed to cry, if tears come. And you're also allowed to not feel anything in particular.
Sometimes we've learned to hide our sadness, to tuck it away quickly so we can keep going. Here, there's nothing to hide. No one is watching. There's only you, and this moment.
And if part of you thinks this is a bit pointless, or wonders whether you're really allowed to be sad over something so small, that part can stay too. There's no such thing as a small sadness.
Settle into a place where you feel sheltered. A couch, your bed, a corner of the floor with a cushion.
If you're a little cold, grab a blanket, a throw, a soft sweater. Sadness can make the body feel cold, and it's good to offer it some warmth.
Let your body sink into whatever is holding it. You don't have to sit up straight or put on a brave face.
Close your eyes if you like, or let your gaze rest on something soft.
Notice the places where your body is supported. The back of your head, your back, your legs. Let them hold a little of your weight, a little more with each out-breath.
[pause 3s]
Breathe the way you're breathing. Maybe your breath is short, or there are sighs. Let them come. A sigh is often the body letting off a little weight.
Feel the air come in. Feel the air go out. Nothing to get right.
If your mind drifts into memories or thoughts, that's okay. You can gently come back to the movement of the air, without blaming yourself.
Now, if you feel like it, try to notice where the sadness lives in your body.

It often has favorite places. The throat, with a lump that tightens. The chest, heavy, as if something were resting on it. The eyes, stinging or burning. Sometimes the stomach, hollow, or the shoulders, slumping.
Take a little tour, without hurrying. And when you find a place where it's clearest, stay with it.
Notice its shape, its size, its density. Is it tight, heavy, empty, warm? Does it move, or is it still?
You don't need to understand it. Just look, with attention that's as gentle as you can make it.
If it feels like too much at any point, you can open your eyes, look around the room, and feel your feet. You're always free to step back.
If you can't find a specific place, that's okay. Sadness is sometimes everywhere and nowhere, like a grey color laid over the whole body. Then you can simply feel your whole body, just as it is.
[pause 3s]
Now let your breath move toward that place. As if each in-breath were bringing it a little air, a little space.
And on the out-breath, don't try to make it leave. Just let it exist. "You can be here."
Often, we tense up around sadness, to contain it, so we don't fall apart. Notice whether there's that kind of tension around it, in your jaw, in your forehead, in your hands.
And see if you can loosen, just a little, whatever is squeezing around it. The sadness can stay. It's only the struggle you're setting down.

Soften your forehead, as if you were smoothing out a sheet. Unclench your teeth, let your tongue rest. Open your hands, palms up if that's comfortable. A body that's a little less tense lets what needs to pass, pass more easily.
[pause 3s]
If tears come, let them. There's nothing weak about them. They rise and fall like waves, and afterward the body is often a little calmer.
If nothing comes, that's fine too. There's no right way to be sad.

Thoughts sometimes come along with sadness. "This will never pass." "I should be over this by now." "I'm too sensitive." Notice them, like heavy clouds. They're part of the weather right now. They don't tell the whole truth about you, or about the future.
Emotions, even heavy ones, change over time. They have their own rhythm, like the seasons, and you don't have to hurry that rhythm along.
Now I'd like to offer you an image. Imagine that someone dear to you is sad, sitting on a bench, or on the edge of a bed.
You come and sit down beside them. You don't say "come on, it'll pass". You don't try to distract them or give them advice.
You're simply there. Your shoulder close to theirs. Maybe your hand on their back. You stay, without hurrying, for as long as it takes.
Feel what it's like to offer that kind of presence.
Maybe notice what happens in your own body as you picture this scene. Some softness, some warmth, a little tenderness. These are resources you already carry inside you.
Maybe you've lived this from the other side. Someone who stayed close to you on a hard night, without saying anything, and whose simple presence changed everything. Remember what that felt like.
[pause 3s]
And now, imagine that this person is you. That you can sit beside your own sadness, the way you would for someone you love.
Not to fix it. Just to keep it company. You, beside yourself.
What would the part of you that comforts say to the part of you that hurts? Maybe nothing. Maybe just: "I'm staying." Let those words, or that silence, do their work.
[pause 3s]
If it's comfortable, place a hand on your heart, or on the spot where the sadness is. Your other hand can rest on your belly, or on your cheek.
Feel the warmth of your hands. Their light weight. Many people find this gesture soothing, simple as it is, like a hug you give yourself.
And offer yourself a few words of support. Choose the ones that ring true for you.
"This is a hard moment."
[pause 3s]
"I'm not the only one who feels this. So many people know this kind of pain."
[pause 3s]
"May I be gentle with myself, right now."
[pause 3s]
"I'll take all the time I need."
[pause 3s]
If these phrases feel strange, just keep your hand where it is, and breathe beneath it. Sometimes the gesture speaks better than words.
This gesture of a hand on the heart comes from self-compassion practices. It doesn't try to erase the pain. It reminds you that you can be on your own side, even in the hard moments.
Now, if you have the energy, one last question, to ask very gently. What is this sadness telling me about what matters to me?
We only grieve what we care about. A person we love. A bond that has been damaged. A project we believed in. A part of ourselves we've left behind.
Your sadness may be the trace of that attachment. The shadow cast by something precious.

If you've lost someone, this sadness speaks of the love that goes on, even when the person is no longer here. If it's a dream slipping away, it tells you how much it meant. Sadness and attachment are often two sides of the same coin.
Let whatever comes, come. A face, a place, a word. And if nothing comes, that's okay. You don't need an answer today.
[pause 3s]
Gently come back to your breath. To the feeling of your hand, if it's still there. To the warmth of the blanket.
The sadness may still be here. Maybe a little lighter, maybe the same. But you didn't leave it alone. You offered it your presence, and you offered that presence to yourself as well.
Notice what it's like to have been present with yourself for these few minutes. Even if it felt imperfect, it was a real act of care.
Take your time coming back. Move your fingers a little. Breathe a little more deeply.
You can stay warm and cozy for a while after this session, if you need to. Make yourself a cup of tea. Send a message to someone you trust. Step outside for some air, even for five minutes.
And if you can, eat something simple and warm today. Taking care of the body is also taking care of the heart.
And be patient with yourself in the days ahead. Sadness sometimes needs to come back a few times before it softens. You can return to this session whenever you feel the need.
Open your eyes when the moment feels right for you.

And if this sadness settles in for a long time, if it lasts for weeks or keeps you from living your daily life, please talk to a doctor or a health professional. Asking for help is also a way of taking care of yourself.

sessions.title: Worry appointment
script: Welcome to your worry appointment. The name might sound strange: why make an appointment with the things that worry us?
Because worries have a habit of showing up whenever they like. In a meeting, in the shower, in the middle of a movie, at three in the morning. And every time, we get swept along.

The idea behind this technique, widely used in cognitive behavioral therapy, is simple. Instead of worrying all day long, you worry on purpose, for a limited time. And the rest of the time, you're allowed to tell your worries: "not now, I'll see you at the next appointment".

Many people find that with a little practice, worries take up less room in their day. Ideally, you'd do this appointment every day at the same time, preferably in the late afternoon, and not right before bed.
Why not right before bed? Because your mind needs a little time to settle afterward. Your bed should stay a place for rest, not for sorting.
If you'd like, grab a sheet of paper and a pen, or open a note on your phone. Writing helps get worries out of your head. But you can also do all of this in your mind.
Sit in a way that keeps you alert but comfortable. Keep your eyes open if you're writing, or close them if you prefer.
Take a calm breath. Plant your feet. Feel your back. The appointment begins.
[pause 3s]
For the next few minutes, you have permission to worry. Really. No need to talk yourself out of it, or to tell yourself it's no big deal.
Let all the worries that are spinning right now come up. The big ones, the small ones, the recurring ones, the new ones, the silly ones too.

Work: a project, a deadline, a tense relationship with a coworker. Money: a bill, an overdraft, an upcoming expense. Health, yours or a loved one's. Family, your relationship, your friends. Your home. The future.
Write them down, or name them silently, one by one. One line, a few words per worry. No details, no solutions for now. Just a list.
If a worry seems too embarrassing or too small to note, note it anyway. Every worry is welcome here. The more honest the list, the more useful the sorting will be.
If it starts to feel like too much, you can slow down, set your pen down, and feel your feet on the floor for a few seconds before carrying on.
[pause 3s]
Keep going. Are there any others, hiding behind the first ones? Things you avoid looking at? If so, add them too.
Notice how your body reacts while you make this list. Maybe some tightening, a quickening. That's normal, and it will settle. Let your out-breath lengthen a little.

Now look at your list as a whole. Sometimes just seeing your worries written down, in black and white, makes them smaller, or clearer. What was going round and round in your head fits, in the end, into a few lines.
[pause 3s]
Now you're going to sort each worry with one single question: is this a real problem, happening now, or a hypothetical problem, one that might happen someday?
A real problem is something like: "my car is making a weird noise", "I haven't answered that email", "I have an unresolved argument with my sister". It's here, today.
A hypothetical problem often starts with "what if". "What if I lose my job." "What if it's a serious illness." "What if my kids don't turn out okay." It isn't happening. It might, perhaps, someday.
Go back through your list from the start, and for each worry, mark an R for real, or an H for hypothetical. If you're not writing, sort them in your mind, to the left or to the right.
A quick test can help: can I do something about this in the next few days? If so, it's probably a real worry. If the answer is "no, I can only wait or imagine", it's probably a hypothetical one.
[pause 3s]
Take your time. Some worries are a mix. "What if my presentation goes badly" is hypothetical, but "I haven't prepared my presentation yet" is real. You can separate them.
This sorting isn't a test. If you're unsure, put a question mark and move on. What matters is seeing more clearly, not being right.
Let's start with the real worries. For each one, look for a concrete next step. Not the whole solution, just the next step.
The car noise: call the garage tomorrow morning. The waiting email: reply in two lines at ten o'clock. The argument: send a message suggesting you talk this weekend.
Make each step very precise. What, and when. If you're writing, note it next to the worry.

If the problem is huge, like a move or a conflict at work, break it down. The next step isn't "resolve the conflict", it's "write three sentences to prepare for the conversation". Small, doable, scheduled.
And if a real problem has no immediate solution, the step can be asking for help, or setting a time to think it over later.
Notice what it's like to turn a vague worry into a small, precise action. Often, the body relaxes a little as soon as it knows what it's going to do.
[pause 3s]

Now for the hypothetical worries. You can't solve these today, because they don't exist yet. Going over and over them doesn't stop them from happening. It just makes you carry their weight in advance.

And often, what we dread doesn't happen the way we imagined. Think of something you were worried about a year ago. Did it happen exactly that way? And if something hard did happen, you faced it with the resources you had at the time.
Take them one by one. Simply acknowledge each one: "This is a worry about the future. It's here because this matters to me."
Then let it be. If you're writing, you can draw a light line through it, or fold the page over on that side. If you're doing this in your mind, imagine placing it on a shelf.
You're not denying it. You're choosing not to deal with it now, because there's nothing to do with it, here, today.
[pause 3s]
If some hypothetical worries resist, ask yourself: is there one small, real thing I can do to prepare, or to take care of myself? If so, move it to the real side. If not, leave it on the shelf.
Over time, you may notice that some hypothetical worries come back often. They're old regulars. You can greet them, without throwing the door wide open.
The appointment is coming to an end. We're going to close it, for real.

If you've been writing, fold your sheet in half, or close the note, and put it away in a drawer, a bag, somewhere separate. If you did it all in your head, imagine closing a notebook and setting it down on a table, far from you.
Tell yourself silently, firmly and kindly: "The appointment is over. See you tomorrow, same time."

Notice the effect of that sentence. Maybe a small relief. Maybe a part of you that doubts: "what if I forget something?". Nothing will be forgotten. It's all on the list, and the list is waiting for you.
[pause 3s]
Now here's the most important instruction, the one that makes this technique work.
During the day, a worry will almost certainly come knocking again. That's normal; they're used to walking in unannounced.
When that happens, don't argue with it. Notice it, and simply tell it: "I see you. We'll talk about it at the next appointment." You can even jot it down quickly on tomorrow's list.
Then go back to what you were doing. In the first few days, this may take a lot of reminders. Over time, many people find their worries wait their turn more patiently.
This isn't avoidance. You're not sweeping your worries under the rug; you're giving them a real appointment. That's exactly what lets your mind loosen its grip on them in between.
[pause 3s]
To finish, come back to the present through your body. Place both feet flat and press them gently into the floor. Feel how solid it is.
Rest your hands on your thighs. Notice their weight, their warmth.
Gently roll your shoulders back, once, twice. Slowly turn your head to one side, then the other. Your body also needs to know the appointment is over.
Let your breath settle. One breath in. One long breath out, releasing your shoulders.
[pause 3s]
Look around you, or open your eyes if they were closed. Choose three things you can see right now, and name them silently.
Listen for one sound, near or far.
[pause 3s]
Your worries are put away, and your next step is clear. The rest of the day belongs to you. And tomorrow, at the same time, your appointment will be waiting.
Thank you for giving yourself this time.
